title: Triangulation Not Confirmation
summary: Triangulation is an evidence practice in which stakeholder interviews, user interviews, observation, benchmarking, analytics, technical constraints and other sources are used to interrogate each other. The aim is not to confirm a common pattern, but to reveal nuances and discrepancies that any single source would miss.
keyFacts: Triangulation differs from conventional multi-method research because sources are used to interrogate each other rather than confirm the same finding from several angles.
A recurring pattern is that stakeholder accounts, user self-report, observed behaviour, competitive benchmarking and technical constraints reveal different parts of the same situation.
The feature X example shows how an apparent time-saving problem can become a more precise error-resolution problem when stakeholder and user evidence are compared.

Research methods named in this practice include stakeholder interviews, user interviews, contextual inquiry, field study, competitive analysis, heuristic evaluation, analytics audit, technical constraints discussions, operator environment audit, domain expert knowledge mapping and legacy system analysis.
Sandbox Experiments matter because prototypes create new reality and allow discovery of what could exist alongside what already exists.

In the Triopsis example, stakeholder interviews, 43 user-interview sessions with 21 participants, 3 in-situ observation sessions, behavioural science and ergonomics research, and benchmarking revealed different operational failures in the same system.

In the Torqeedo example, legacy system analysis, 12 sea-trial observation sessions with 15 captains, a controlled experiment with 24 subjects, eye tracking with 7 subjects and satisfaction feedback from 15 captains each contributed different evidence.

In the Gexcon example, 24 user-interview sessions, 23 in-situ observation sessions, 9 stakeholder-interview sessions, benchmarking of 12 systems, and analysis of 102 tasks formed distinct evidence sources.
The Squaremind example is sequential: pre-engagement client test data, field observation, structured post-redesign testing, clinical judgement and clinic-demo observation were used in sequence.
The practice explicitly excludes cases where only one source was interrogated or where artefacts were checked only for internal coherence.

bodySections.heading: Triangulation Uses Evidence Sources Against Each Other
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Triangulation is Creative Navy's practice of using multiple evidence sources against each other so that discrepancies, rather than agreement alone, reveal what is operationally important. Stakeholder accounts, user interviews, observation, competitive analysis, technical constraints and other sources are treated as evidence sources that can interrogate one another.

The signal in triangulation is often the discrepancy. Agreement between sources can be useful, but a result that every source confirms is less informative than a divergence that shows what one source can see and another source cannot. The finding is therefore not simply a confirmed fact. It is a richer understanding of the product, the market, the competition, user value, commercial positioning and technical build requirements.

bodySections.heading: How Triangulation Differs From Conventional Multi-Method Research
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Conventional multi-method research often uses different methods to increase confidence in a finding by confirming it from multiple angles. Triangulation as Creative Navy practises it uses different methods to interrogate each other, with discrepancies treated as informative findings.

A simple example is a feature that stakeholders and users both describe as important. Stakeholders may say feature X matters because users want to save time. Users may say feature X matters because they are under time pressure and each mistake takes a long time to resolve. These can sound like the same finding, but triangulation separates them. The underlying problem is error resolution time, not time saving in general.

That nuance can then be taken back to stakeholders to ask what it changes about the feature. It can be taken to competitive analysis to examine how competing products prevent errors or make correction faster. It can be taken to technical-constraint discussions to examine what could be done differently. Each source shines a different light on the nuance, and the nuance is visible because the sources are used against each other rather than used to confirm one another.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Sources Used in Triangulation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's triangulation practice can involve stakeholder interviews, user interviews, contextual inquiry, field study, competitive analysis, heuristic evaluation, analytics audit, technical constraints discussions, operator environment audit, domain expert knowledge mapping, legacy system analysis and other evidence sources. The value is not located in any single method. The value comes from how the sources are compared, challenged and sequenced.

User observation has a specific role in triangulation. Having users teach the team to use a system, and having team members attempt to do the job as a user, can reveal silent patterns, conscious process models, expectations about how the process should work, learning histories, changes in difficulty as users become more experienced and the emotional weighting of these issues. Observation can also reveal what users would or would not be capable of if the system were different.

Context of use is part of the evidence, not background decoration. A tool is embedded in a context, and many opportunities for value sit in how the tool integrates with that context. This is why triangulation can include operator environment audits, field study and domain expert knowledge mapping alongside interviews and benchmarks.

bodySections.heading: Sandbox Experiments Add Possible Futures to Observed Reality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses Sandbox Experiments as part of discovery because discovery is not limited to observing what already exists. Prototypes create new reality and allow the team to discover what could exist alongside what does exist.

This changes the role of evidence. A prototype can be used as an evidence source that interrogates user accounts, stakeholder assumptions, technical constraints and competitive patterns. It does not merely test a proposed answer. It can reveal that an existing description of the problem was incomplete because users respond differently when a different operational possibility is placed in front of them.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis Shows Role-Specific Failures Inside One Workforce-Management System
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Triopsis workforce management SaaS example, five evidence sources were used against each other rather than used to confirm common patterns. Stakeholder interviews with 5 stakeholders surfaced competing organisational priorities: throughput, stability, safety and demo performance. These priorities did not confirm a single direction; they revealed structural tensions.

User interviews in 43 sessions with 21 participants showed that the same interface failed three roles differently. Schedulers described speed problems. Operations managers described exception visibility problems. Technicians described clarity and confirmation problems. These were not the same problem seen from different angles; they were different operational failures in the same system.

In-situ observation in 3 sessions revealed behaviour under real-time pressure that interviews could not surface, including hesitation patterns, repeated checking and error patterns such as incorrect sequencing and duplicate assignments. Behavioural science and ergonomics research helped interpret the mechanisms behind the observed patterns. Benchmarking provided competitive context and identified gaps the client had not recognised as problems.

bodySections.heading: Torqeedo Shows Evidence Sources With Different Roles
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Torqeedo maritime HMI example, the evidence sources did not simply provide different perspectives on the same questions. Legacy system analysis revealed compensation patterns: how captains had learned to work around information fragmentation. This pattern was visible through analysis of the existing system, not through interviews or observation alone.

Sea-trial observation with 15 captains across 12 sessions revealed scanning patterns and physical interaction failures that appeared under real maritime conditions, including vibration, glare from cold water and night operations. A controlled experiment with 24 subjects quantified what observation had suggested: captains identified key energy states 50% faster with the new interface. Eye tracking in sea trials with 7 subjects directly counted glance reductions during manoeuvres. Captain satisfaction feedback from 15 captains confirmed the direction of the qualitative findings with structured feedback.

Each source did something the others could not. The controlled experiment quantified what observation had suggested. Eye tracking measured what the controlled experiment had established in principle. Legacy analysis explained why the patterns appeared that the sea trials revealed.

bodySections.heading: Gexcon Shows Triangulation in an Expert Software Domain
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Gexcon CFD simulation software example, six evidence sources were used against each other across the Sandbox Experiments phase. Domain learning included studying manuals, tutorials and internal training materials, running controlled tests inside the application, and two intensive four-hour stakeholder sessions to reverse-engineer the workflow sequence.

User interviews in 24 sessions surfaced how different user types experienced the same interface differently, including senior CFD engineers, safety analysts, process engineers, newer engineers and risk managers. In-situ observations in 23 sessions showed how engineers navigated non-linearly between configuration, verification and interpretation, and how they managed dense state within a single environment rather than across distributed screens.

Stakeholder interviews in 9 sessions produced organisational and product priorities that did not align cleanly with user research, a discrepancy connected in the notes to the blanks phenomenon operating inside the client organisation. Competitor benchmarking across 12 systems identified structural patterns and specific gaps the client had not recognised as problems. Feature and task analysis documented 102 tasks with goals, frequency, difficulty and actions, providing the empirical backbone for a specific requirement structure.

bodySections.heading: The Swiss Petrol Station Operator Example Shows Transaction Coding Interrogating Observation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Swiss petrol station operator example, the Sandbox Experiments phase combined qualitative evidence with a coded operational corpus. Forty hours of structured observation and 24 interviews produced a qualitative picture of where cashiers experienced friction. These findings were used against a coded dataset of 532 transactions, categorised by type and complexity.

The sources disagreed in informative ways. Interview self-report and observation suggested that combined transactions were the primary source of cashier stress. Transaction coding showed that the frequency and complexity distribution was different from how cashiers described it. Certain transaction types that cashiers rarely mentioned were disproportionately represented in error-recovery sequences.

The discrepancy was the finding. Cashiers had normalised compensating behaviours, including personal shortcuts around field-ordering inconsistencies, to the point where those behaviours no longer registered as problems in self-report or even in observed-behaviour description. Coding made the pattern visible because it counted the events without relying on cashier recognition.

bodySections.heading: Akrivia Health Shows Triangulation Across Institutional Contexts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Akrivia Health clinical research platform example, the relevant evidence came from three institutionally distinct user groups using the same platform: NHS analysts, academic research teams and pharmaceutical research staff. These groups operated under different institutional constraints. NHS analysts maintained strict governance boundaries between research and operational use. Academic teams worked through lengthy ethics and data access approvals before touching real patient records. Pharmaceutical teams had more exploratory freedom early in studies but strict audit and reporting obligations later.

Creative Navy did not aggregate these groups into a single researcher persona. The groups were used against each other. The NHS group's governance boundaries revealed requirements for clear workflow state. The academic group's approval timelines made related issues visible from a different angle. The pharmaceutical group's audit obligations revealed requirements for query history and decision traceability.

The critical finding was that confusion concentrated at handover points between governance stages and between team members. No single group's account of the failure was complete. The full picture came from triangulating across institutional positions.

bodySections.heading: WCO IPM Shows Geographic and Institutional Triangulation in a Live Enforcement Platform
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the World Customs Organization IPM example, the Sandbox Experiments phase involved three user groups with different operational relationships to the same platform: frontline inspection officers checking shipments against alerts under time pressure, intelligence analysts needing structured access to case histories and seizure patterns, and rights holder brand protection and legal teams needing clear paths to file information and monitor enforcement activity.

Research combined interviews and workflow mapping with WCO teams and remote observation across selected member administrations. Validation included 47 usability testing participants from Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria and Spain. The geographic spread was not treated as statistical coverage. It was used to interrogate whether design decisions that worked in one administrative and linguistic context would hold in other operational contexts.

The discrepancies were findings. A status indicator that was clear in one context was ambiguous in another. Terminology normalised in European customs practice required explicit labelling in Central Asian contexts. Progressive disclosure assumptions that held for experienced officers failed for newer users in administrations with less institutional IPR enforcement history. The result was not a design validated across five countries, but a design stress-tested against five different operational contexts and revised where discrepancies exposed fragility.

bodySections.heading: Squaremind Shows Sequential Triangulation Across Failure Data, Observation, Testing, Clinical Judgement and Commercial Observation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device example, five sources were assembled sequentially rather than gathered in parallel. The first source was the client's own pre-engagement test: 14 users and 2 completions. This client-reported background data established the scale of the failure and an age-stratified failure pattern, but it could not explain the structure of the problem.

Creative Navy then ran 4 unstructured field observation sessions in France. These sessions were not structured as measurement because the existing system was too poor to measure usefully. Field observation produced situated understanding of the relationship between patient and screen, the spatial context of the scan, and observable confusion as body movement before abandonment.

Structured post-redesign testing in London with 12 users and Paris with 17 users, co-conducted with an independent dermatologist hired by Creative Navy, became the primary measurement source. It recorded binary completion, timed recovery and a failure-point catalogue. The independent dermatologist's clinical judgement interrogated the testing data at the boundary between usability and clinical appropriateness. Creative Navy's direct observation of 5 of the 9 clinic demos after the redesign then tested the findings against a commercial condition: buyers walking through the patient experience to decide whether real patients could complete the process. All 5 observed demos resulted in purchase.

bodySections.heading: Additional Examples Show Different Triangulation Structures
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The European industrial automation engagement shows sources built rather than accepted. Five personas were built from direct research sessions covering six individuals across three role types. A co-authored requirements table forced unstated assumptions into writing. Four competitors were benchmarked. Operators were observed in situ at the client's facility. These observations are engagement-specific rather than general claims about the industry, and the product is still in development, so no outcome is claimed.

In the Streetec example, requirements for the kntrl 2 control system for aftermarket automotive air suspension were developed as a collaborative artefact. Streetec's functional specification was reorganised into a two-column table pairing each Creative Navy question with Streetec's written answer, function by function. This was combined with unstructured competitive benchmarking of three competing products, an internal design check with n=2 on wireframes that was not user research, and testing of the production product installed in a real car with 32 participants.

In the AIT heat pump controller example, Creative Navy benchmarked 10 thermostat and heat pump control interfaces against 15 features. AIT supplied its own competitor visualisation, covering its current controller plus six competitor systems across nine interface themes with 76 screenshots. Published human-factors literature formed a third leg by settling touch-target and legibility questions neither benchmark could settle. The engagement had no user research, no installer interviews, no contextual inquiry, no field observation, no usability testing and no personas built from research; the two personas were supplied by AIT.

In the MDU ship motion monitoring example, three sources disagreed about yaw. The written specification named roll, pitch and yaw as primary metrics. The Modbus register map had no yaw register. The manufacturer's spoken answers were uncertain that yaw could ever be shown reliably. Creative Navy raised the disagreement in the requirements table rather than designing around the specification, and the review removed the yaw card. The user-side evidence base was one external advisor, a serving master and chief engineer present in review calls.

bodySections.heading: Examples Where Evidence Types Must Be Kept in Their Correct Category
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Egma example, five internal functions gave five accounts of the failing lens configurator that did not agree with one another. Egma's CEO reported that the configurator was restraining revenue because customers did not appear to find all available configurations and looked elsewhere; this was the CEO's diagnosis of the business, not a measured finding. A second evidence leg came from 17 optometrists across four rounds of structured interviews, semi-structured interviews and wireframe-feedback sessions. This was not usability testing, not contextual inquiry and not observation in stores. A heatmap produced during the engagement identified three regions of the order form where users hesitated. The finding is tool-generated and reflects real behaviour; the capture method is not on record, so it is reported as an observation rather than a measurement.

In the Oceaneering dispatch panel example, Creative Navy learned the domain from a predecessor's 92-page specification, published AGV literature, a publicly sourced staff orientation film and six interviews with people adjacent to the users rather than the users themselves, plus one hospital project team. The sources disagreed usefully: the orientation film depicted a clean automated hall, while a staff software engineer described hospitals that look organised but are not, with dirty areas and other objects left standing around. No dispatch operator was interviewed, no depot was visited, and no field research or contextual inquiry took place; the operating context was documented and client-stated, not observed by Creative Navy.

In the Raymarine engagement, triangulation was made auditable by declaring four evidence classes and labelling every decision in a register with the evidence class it rested on: comparative prototype evidence, scenario observation, design reasoning and technical dependency. This made it visible which conclusions depended on which evidence class and which conclusions would survive if one source were withdrawn.

bodySections.heading: Handheld Command-and-Control, Maritime VTS and Visioncheckout Show Discrepancy-Led Reasoning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, the benchmark covered 32 systems, 21 of them analysed in depth, across nine research dimensions. Real-time strategy games were used as a functional model for fast decision-making at the client's own suggestion in its brief. The client's brief framed the handheld as a version of the existing product. The expert review concluded that it was a different product: not a scaled-down laptop, but a distinct product solving a related problem. Creative Navy had no primary field evidence in this engagement; the review reasoned from the client's brief, the client's observations of its own users, published literature and hands-on use of the running product.

In the maritime VTS engagement, ten research sessions were used against each other rather than in parallel: six stakeholder interviews covering product strategy, VTS, communications, RIS, frontend architecture and commercial priorities, and four operator sessions, two with supervised workstation observation. Six recorded disagreements were resolved rather than averaged. Three multidisciplinary disagreements were resolved in review: panel mobility against target visibility, one alert inbox against operational meaning, and visual certainty against defensible provenance. In all three, the specialised behaviour won.

In the visioncheckout example, three sources were used against each other on the keycard finding. Field observation showed an overcharge scenario: an employee intending to pay by credit card forgot to present the employee card for the discount and paid more than intended. The client-stated behaviour explained why this happened: 90–95% of users paid by keycard, and placing the keycard paid immediately where balance was available. The same client statement also created the counter-argument: if 90–95% paid by keycard, changing the behaviour would affect nearly every guest. The discrepancy between what the product was designed to do and what it cost a guest was the finding. The same engagement also used a competitive benchmark of thirteen comparators in three tiers, with every claim labelled as verified, high, medium, low or analysis.

bodySections.heading: Triangulation Depends on Persistence and Access as Well as Method Choice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's triangulation practice is shaped by how evidence is pursued, not only by which methods are listed. The same activity can produce different results depending on whether the team persists to find the right participants, returns for a second session, asks a daring question, gains access to software not publicly available for benchmarking, or asks developers to reconsider technical constraints.

Developer constraint discussions are not treated as a claim that the design team knows better. They are a way to test whether a changed perspective creates value for the developers themselves. In the same way, access to real users through Creative Navy can produce information the client organisation does not already have, because users are often more open with a third party than with their own provider.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Non-Examples Prevent Triangulation From Becoming a Catch-All Label
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
KISPE is not treated as a triangulation example for this page. KISPE cross-checked six design artefacts against one fixture for internal consistency. That is coherence checking, not triangulation between user, stakeholder or research sources.

Assemblio is also not treated as a triangulation example. That engagement had a single research source Creative Navy did not control: research performed by Assemblio, without Creative Navy control over recruitment, questions or recording. A designer interrogating one source hard can be a real practice, but it is not triangulation. Triangulation requires sources used against each other.

Several examples on this page carry explicit limits. AIT and MDU had no user research and do not support user-validation claims. Egma's heatmap is an observation rather than a measurement. Oceaneering's operating context was documented and client-stated, not observed by Creative Navy. Streetec's internal check with n=2 on wireframes was not user research, while the later 32-participant work involved unassisted tasks on a finished product installed in a real car. These distinctions are part of the evidence practice: triangulation is only useful when each evidence source is kept in its correct category.

strongClaims: Triangulation in Creative Navy's evidence practice uses sources against each other rather than using multiple methods only to confirm common patterns.
Discrepancies between evidence sources are treated as findings because they reveal what individual sources cannot see.

The Triopsis example used stakeholder interviews, user interviews, in-situ observation, behavioural science and ergonomics research, and benchmarking to reveal role-specific operational failures and source discrepancies.
The Torqeedo example used legacy system analysis, sea-trial observation, a controlled experiment, eye tracking and satisfaction feedback, with each evidence source performing a different role.

The Gexcon example used six evidence sources, including domain learning, 24 user-interview sessions, 23 in-situ observations, 9 stakeholder-interview sessions, benchmarking of 12 systems, and documentation of 102 tasks.

The Squaremind example is sequential triangulation across client-reported pre-engagement test data, Creative Navy field observation, structured post-redesign testing, independent dermatologist judgement and clinic-demo observation.
KISPE and Assemblio are not triangulation examples for this page because KISPE involved coherence checking and Assemblio involved one research source that Creative Navy did not control.
AIT and MDU evidence supports design reasoning but not user validation because neither engagement had user research.
weakerClaims: The feature X example shows that apparent agreement between stakeholders and users can hide a more precise problem: error resolution time rather than general time saving.
Egma's heatmap is reported as an observation rather than a measurement because the capture method is not on record.
limitations: Triangulation on this page means sources used against each other; it does not include coherence checking between artefacts or intensive interrogation of a single evidence source.
Some examples support design reasoning rather than user validation, including AIT and MDU.
The Egma heatmap is an observation rather than a measurement because the capture method is not on record.
The Oceaneering operating context was documented and client-stated, not observed by Creative Navy; no dispatch operator was interviewed and no depot was visited.
The industrial automation engagement is not an outcome example because the product is in development.
The Streetec internal design check was internal, n=2, on wireframes, and not user research.

The handheld command-and-control review had no primary field evidence from Creative Navy; it reasoned from the client's brief, the client's observations, published literature and hands-on use of the running product.
